prediction.likelyOutcome: Covenant has a moderately favorable position heading to trial: strong extrinsic evidence (the LOI, the broker's email, and Empower's own delay/self-interested conduct) supports both an unsatisfied-condition-precedent theory and an alternative prior-material-breach theory, either of which would justify rescission and return of the $96,291.09 deposit. But the trial court's own ambiguity finding means this is a genuine jury question, and Empower's breach/fraud counterclaims — while weak on the merits as described — carry unquantified exposure because no rent or term-value figures are in the record. Net expected value favors Covenant, centered on partial-to-full recovery of the deposit.

outcome.description: After a four-day jury trial the jury found Section 3(c) was a condition precedent that Empower failed to satisfy; the trial court rendered judgment declaring the lease abrogated and ordered Empower to pay Covenant $96,291.09 in damages (the deposit), $611,491.45 in attorney's fees, and $135,000 in conditional appellate fees. The court of appeals held Section 3(c) is a covenant, not a condition precedent, reversed the entire judgment, rendered take-nothing on the condition-precedent declarations, and remanded the remaining declarations, the damages and fee awards, and Empower's breach-of-contract counterclaim.
